title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
abstract: The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.
comment: 24 pages. Third paper of the series "Classification of Bipartite Observables" by the same authors

bite.hook: Quantum error correction and pure model theory are mathematically identical: simplicity theory is error correction.
tldr: Mapped the infinite Pauli group directly to the random graph paradigm from model theory.
Analyzed stabilizer codes, Clifford circuits, and syndromes using Shelah's classification theory and bipartite observables.
Proved that mixed states give both structures the tree property of the second kind, though via fundamentally different probes.
bite.whyItMatters: Bridging abstract mathematical logic with quantum computing unlocks decades of classification theory to help design and understand quantum error-correcting codes.
bite.eli5: Mathematicians study infinite networks where any random connection can happen. It turns out that tracking and fixing errors on quantum bits follows the exact same hidden rules as these infinite random graphs.

glossary.shortDef: Group generated by single-qubit Pauli matrices and phase factors, fundamental to quantum coding.
glossary.eli5Def: A collection of basic quantum operations used to flip bits or detect errors in quantum computers.

glossary.shortDef: A unique countable homogeneous structure built by gluing together a class of finite structures.
glossary.eli5Def: The ultimate giant structure you get when you piece together all possible smaller toy models of a specific kind.

glossary.shortDef: A quantum error-correcting code defined as the simultaneous +1 eigenspace of an abelian Pauli subgroup.
glossary.eli5Def: A quantum safety net that detects if data got scrambled without looking at the secret data directly.
